video_title: One Type of Post-Quantum Cryptography Is Most Popular. Why Is Crypto Trying Out Three?
gist: NEAR Protocol co-founder Ilia and Ledger CTO Charles walk through crypto's post-quantum migration in concrete technical and policy detail: an AI-accelerated cryptanalysis breakthrough compressed the threat timeline, the ecosystem has fragmented into three incompatible NIST-approved signature schemes (NEAR/Algorand on MLDSA, Bitcoin/Ethereum leaning hash-based, Solana headed to Falcon) instead of converging like the rest of cryptography, and Bitcoin faces an unresolved, high-stakes decision on whether to let Satoshi-era coins be stolen, freeze them, or freeze-and-tail-emit them into new supply.

insights.claim: In roughly March/April of the prior ~8 months, Google published research showing a dramatically improved (Shor's-algorithm-adjacent) technique for recovering private keys from public keys, but withheld the actual algorithm and published only a zero-knowledge proof that it existed, out of concern about how powerful it was.
insights.speaker: Ilia
insights.so_what: The bottleneck for breaking blockchain cryptography is shrinking on the algorithmic side, not just the hardware (qubit-count) side -- this compresses the effective migration timeline for every chain still using ECDSA/EdDSA.

insights.claim: After Google withheld its key-recovery algorithm, an industry-run competition challenged AI systems to independently rediscover it, and the algorithm was found and replicated within about 48 hours, with continued improvement since -- illustrating that AI is now materially accelerating cryptanalytic research.
insights.speaker: Ilia
insights.so_what: AI-assisted cryptanalysis is a new, fast-moving variable in the quantum-risk timeline that most market timelines for 'quantum threat to crypto' do not price in.

insights.claim: NIST issued a formal 2024 mandate to migrate to post-quantum cryptography, but the crypto industry's dominant reaction at the time was that migration was not urgent because a capable quantum computer seemed far off; that complacency broke specifically after Google's late-March quantum/algorithmic breakthrough.
insights.speaker: Charles
insights.so_what: Marks a clear before/after inflection point investors can use to date when 'quantum resistance' became a live, board-level priority for crypto infrastructure rather than a distant compliance item.

insights.claim: Neither guest will commit to a hardware quantum-computer timeline -- both note that '5 years away' has been the industry line for 20 years -- but both argue conviction has genuinely risen because investment in quantum computing has roughly 10x'd in recent years, multiple qubit-stabilization technology paths are showing progress, and AI is accelerating the physics/materials-science research required.
insights.speaker: Charles
insights.so_what: Treat 'no confirmed quantum computer yet' as a weak reason for complacency: the risk model should track algorithmic efficiency and R&D investment trendlines, not just a hardware milestone that keeps sliding.

insights.claim: The widely-cited 'harvest now, decrypt later' threat -- attackers capturing encrypted internet traffic today to decrypt once quantum computers exist -- does not apply to blockchains themselves, because blockchains generally do not use symmetric encryption on-chain; the blockchain-specific quantum risk is signature forgery, not decryption of stored data.
insights.speaker: Charles
insights.so_what: Corrects a common but imprecise framing of blockchain quantum risk; investors evaluating chain-level quantum readiness should focus on signature-scheme migration status, not encryption.

insights.claim: Despite blockchains lacking on-chain encryption, a real harvest-now risk still exists indirectly: users' public keys are routinely transmitted to RPC endpoints, wallets, and exchange backends over currently-vulnerable transport encryption, so attackers can already be harvesting public keys today to extract private keys later once quantum capability arrives.
insights.speaker: Ilia
insights.so_what: Public-key exposure via infrastructure (not just on-chain visibility) is an underappreciated attack surface; wallet/RPC providers upgrading their own transport encryption is part of the quantum-readiness picture, not just chain-level signature schemes.

insights.claim: Charles rejects the common claim that only a small subset of Bitcoin (often cited as roughly 5 million BTC with exposed on-chain public keys from address reuse) is quantum-vulnerable; he argues essentially all Bitcoin public keys should be treated as already public/exposed because they pass through many backends, logs, and networks even when not literally posted on-chain.
insights.speaker: Charles
insights.so_what: Any Bitcoin quantum-risk sizing that relies on the 'only reused-address coins are vulnerable' figure likely understates total exposure; treat the addressable at-risk supply as much larger than the commonly cited number.
insights.quote: Sometimes I hear that only like I don't know five millions of bitcoin are vulnerable because their public key is on chain. This is a very bad argument.

insights.claim: NEAR's founding architectural decision -- decoupling accounts from any single cryptographic scheme by modeling them like a Google/Apple account with pluggable 'access keys' -- gave it a structural head start on post-quantum migration versus Bitcoin, Ethereum, and Solana, which each bake one specific cryptography directly into how an address maps to a private key.
insights.speaker: Ilia
insights.so_what: Chain architecture choices made years before quantum risk was salient are now producing meaningfully different migration costs and timelines -- a structural advantage that isn't visible from token price or TVL alone.

insights.claim: A few months before this recording, NEAR went to mainnet with post-quantum (MLDSA) signature support, which Ilia states is, to his knowledge, the first time users could hold and secure assets on a major blockchain with a post-quantum-secure key.
insights.speaker: Ilia
insights.so_what: A concrete, checkable first-mover claim in the post-quantum blockchain race; worth tracking whether ecosystem tooling (wallets, custodians, exchanges) actually adopts NEAR's PQ signature support at pace.

insights.claim: NEAR's new post-quantum support only covers user account access/signing, not the chain's own consensus layer, which still relies on traditional ECDSA because consensus needs the fastest, smallest signatures possible to hit NEAR's 200-600 millisecond block-time targets; no post-quantum scheme yet exists that is simultaneously fast, cheap, and small enough for high-throughput consensus.
insights.speaker: Ilia
insights.so_what: A genuine unsolved gap: 'post-quantum blockchain' claims should be checked for whether they cover user signatures only or the full consensus stack -- consensus-layer PQ migration is a harder, still-open research problem.

insights.claim: Because NEAR Intents lets users custody and sign for assets on 30+ other chains (Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana, Tron, etc.) from a single NEAR account via MPC, securing the NEAR account with post-quantum cryptography only protects those other-chain assets 'with an asterisk' -- true protection still requires each underlying chain to complete its own migration.
insights.speaker: Ilia
insights.so_what: Aggregation/abstraction layers marketed as a one-stop quantum-safety solution don't eliminate the need for every underlying chain to migrate; investors should discount 'quantum-safe via abstraction' claims accordingly.

insights.claim: On the day of this recording, NEAR announced a pilot with Safeheron and other partners -- including banks, custodians, and regulators -- to test post-quantum multi-party computation (MPC), which Ilia says has not previously existed in production for any chain.
insights.speaker: Ilia
insights.so_what: A concrete near-term catalyst/product milestone for NEAR in institutional custody infrastructure; watch for consortium participants and whether other custodians adopt the same MPC scheme.

insights.claim: Ilia argues the ecosystem should converge on MLDSA specifically because it is likely the only NIST-standardized post-quantum algorithm that supports cryptographic multi-party computation (MPC), which institutional custody depends on -- though both guests caveat that PQ-MPC-on-MLDSA is very new research that has not yet 'passed the test of time.'
insights.speaker: Ilia
insights.so_what: If institutional custody depends on MPC compatibility, MLDSA has a structural advantage over Falcon and Sphinx (SPHINCS+) for that use case specifically -- but the underlying PQ-MPC construction itself is an unproven, early-stage risk to monitor.

themes.theme: Algorithm Fragmentation: Lattice vs. Hash-Based vs. Falcon

insights.claim: NIST standardized three post-quantum signature algorithms -- two lattice-based (MLDSA/Dilithium and Falcon) and one hash-based (Sphinx (SPHINCS+)) -- and outside of blockchain, essentially the entire rest of cryptography (banking, TLS, defense, identity systems) has converged near-unanimously on MLDSA, with no real debate; blockchain is the one domain where the choice remains contested.
insights.speaker: Charles
insights.so_what: Blockchain's algorithm fragmentation is an industry outlier versus every other cryptography-dependent sector, implying the split is driven by something beyond pure security engineering (see competitive-dynamics insight below).
insights.quote: In defense, in banking, in TLS they all use the same algorithm which is MLDSA. For the blockchain world, this is where this discussion is happening... this is quite weird to see.

insights.claim: Bitcoin and Ethereum's developer communities are leaning toward hash-based signatures (Sphinx (SPHINCS+) variants) mainly for conservatism: hash functions have decades of real-world security track record, whereas lattice-based cryptography, though academically ~30-40 years old, has never actually been deployed in production until now, and some practitioners worry AI-assisted cryptanalysis could eventually find weaknesses in it.
insights.speaker: Charles
insights.so_what: The two largest chains by market cap are optimizing for cryptographic conservatism over efficiency -- expect Bitcoin/Ethereum PQ migrations to ship larger, slower signatures than NEAR/Algorand's MLDSA approach.

insights.claim: Raw Sphinx (SPHINCS+) as NIST-standardized is impractical for blockchains because it produces very large signatures that are expensive to compute and verify; Bitcoin and Ethereum implementers are expected to use smaller-parameter hash-based variants instead, which typically trade away either statelessness (requiring the wallet to track signer state) or unlimited signature counts per key.
insights.speaker: Charles
insights.so_what: Watch for exactly which hash-based parameter set Bitcoin/Ethereum ultimately choose -- stateful signing schemes introduce new operational failure modes (state-tracking bugs can lead to catastrophic key reuse) that wallets and custodians must engineer around.
insights.quote: It's just very bad to implement it because it produces very very large signatures. It cost a lot to compute them, it cost a lot to verify them.

insights.claim: Solana is expected to adopt Falcon -- the second lattice-based NIST standard -- specifically because it produces the shortest available post-quantum signatures, prioritizing latency preservation over the conservatism argument that's driving Bitcoin and Ethereum's choice.
insights.speaker: Charles
insights.so_what: Each major chain's PQ algorithm choice is being driven by its core value proposition (Solana=latency, NEAR/Algorand=MPC+efficiency, BTC/ETH=conservatism) rather than a shared security standard -- meaning the ecosystem will permanently run three incompatible PQ signature schemes.

insights.claim: Charles floats his own hypothesis for why blockchain is fragmenting on post-quantum algorithms while every other cryptography-dependent industry converged on one: beyond genuine conservatism, each blockchain may be treating a distinct PQ approach as a competitive-differentiation lever against rival chains.
insights.speaker: Charles
insights.so_what: If algorithm choice is partly a branding/competitive decision rather than a pure security one, expect continued fragmentation even after any one scheme proves superior -- de-risking any single 'winner-take-all' PQ-standard investment thesis in crypto infrastructure.
insights.quote: Every single blockchain is competing against each other, and having something different to propose to the users can be a competitive advantage as well.

insights.claim: Ilia agrees competitive dynamics are likely driving the fragmentation, but argues the ecosystem should actively converge on fewer PQ standards anyway, because every additional scheme multiplies the integration burden across wallets, custodians, and exchanges, and dilutes the collective security benefit of many independent reviewers auditing one shared implementation.
insights.speaker: Ilia
insights.so_what: Infrastructure providers serving multiple chains (wallets, custodians, bridges) face rising compliance/engineering cost from algorithm fragmentation regardless of which scheme 'wins' -- a durable tailwind for firms that specialize in cross-scheme PQ tooling.

insights.claim: Because there is 'no real debate' that a multi-chain wallet provider must support all three NIST-standardized PQ algorithms (MLDSA, Falcon, and hash-based variants) to serve users across the ecosystem, algorithm fragmentation directly and permanently increases the engineering and security-audit surface area for hardware wallet and custody providers.
insights.speaker: Charles
insights.so_what: Custody/wallet infrastructure vendors will carry structurally higher R&D and audit costs than a single-standard world would imply -- a factor to weight when assessing margins or security risk at firms like Ledger.

insights.claim: Ledger's current secure element chips were designed for banking and identity use cases and do not natively support post-quantum signature algorithms in hardware; Ledger's present PQ support (MLDSA, used by NEAR) runs at the firmware level instead, which works and keeps the private key inside the secure element, but is slower and forgoes some of the chip's built-in hardware-acceleration and security properties.
insights.speaker: Charles
insights.so_what: Current-generation Ledger PQ signing should be expected to be noticeably slower than legacy-curve signing, and users should not assume full hardware-level PQ security guarantees until next-gen secure elements ship.

insights.claim: Charles states Ledger has already shipped firmware-level MLDSA support (used for NEAR), which he calls 'a first in the world' for signing a post-quantum blockchain transaction on a hardware wallet secure device, and plans to extend firmware-level support to hash-based and Falcon signatures next.
insights.speaker: Charles
insights.so_what: A concrete, dated first-mover claim in hardware-wallet PQ support that's independently checkable against Ledger's product releases and SDK documentation.

insights.claim: Ledger's next-generation secure element will support MLDSA and improved hash-based signatures directly in hardware for higher speed and security, but Falcon -- the algorithm expected to be used by Solana -- will NOT be supported at the hardware level even in the next generation and will remain firmware-implemented, meaning Solana-related signing will structurally lag NEAR/Algorand-style MLDSA signing on Ledger devices for the foreseeable future.
insights.speaker: Charles
insights.so_what: A specific, checkable hardware-roadmap claim implying a persistent UX/performance gap for Solana users on Ledger relative to NEAR/Algorand users -- worth revisiting when Ledger's next-gen devices actually ship.

insights.claim: Charles frames the question 'is Ledger quantum-safe' as effectively ill-posed in isolation: Ledger can implement every standardized post-quantum algorithm, but a user's assets are only as quantum-safe as the underlying blockchain itself, so hardware-wallet PQ-readiness is necessary but not sufficient -- real protection requires the chain, custodians, and wallet to migrate together.
insights.speaker: Charles
insights.so_what: Marketing claims of 'quantum-safe hardware wallet' should be treated skeptically unless paired with the specific underlying chain's own migration status -- the weakest link in the stack determines real-world safety.

insights.claim: Ledger's current MLDSA implementation does not yet benefit from all of the secure element's dedicated hardware countermeasures against physical key-extraction attacks (e.g., a stolen device) the way legacy-curve signing does, because those accelerators/countermeasures aren't yet built for the new algorithm at the firmware level -- though Charles still assesses practical key extraction as 'very very difficult.'
insights.speaker: Charles
insights.so_what: A specific, disclosed security trade-off in current-generation PQ hardware wallet support that security-conscious institutional users should factor into custody decisions until next-gen hardware ships.

insights.claim: For Bitcoin's dormant/unmigrated coins (including Satoshi's roughly 1M+ BTC), there are three mutually exclusive policy options once quantum-capable attacks become feasible: (1) do nothing and let them be stolen, risking a major liquidity/market shock; (2) freeze them permanently, shrinking effective circulating supply from ~21M toward roughly 16M BTC, which raises private-property objections; or (3) freeze them AND 'tail-emit' the frozen amount back into future miner rewards, expanding Bitcoin's total eventual issuance from ~21M to roughly 24-26M BTC.
insights.speaker: Charles
insights.so_what: This is a concrete, quantifiable tail-risk framework for Bitcoin's supply cap itself -- any of these three outcomes would materially change either Bitcoin's effective circulating supply or its long-run issuance schedule, both first-order inputs to a BTC valuation model.
insights.quote: Instead of emitting only 1 million bitcoin until [the year] 2176, you will emit like four to five million bitcoin that were not migrated.

insights.claim: Charles's personal preference is option 3 (freeze plus tail-emission) because he judges doing nothing as too catastrophic -- a quantum-capable attacker dumping millions of BTC would 'simply destroy the project' -- and because tail-emission has the side benefit of helping fund Bitcoin's long-run 'security budget' (the concern that miner revenue becomes insufficient as the block subsidy shrinks toward zero).
insights.speaker: Charles
insights.so_what: Links two previously separate Bitcoin tail risks -- quantum-vulnerable dormant coins and the long-run miner security-budget problem -- into a single proposed policy fix; if adopted, this would be one of the most consequential monetary-policy changes in Bitcoin's history.

insights.claim: Ilia largely agrees that tail-emitting unmigrated coins would be an efficient way to address both the quantum-theft risk and Bitcoin's separate long-run security-budget problem simultaneously, calling it 'killing two birds with one stone,' though he considers this outcome the least politically likely of the three options and does not hold a strong personal view.
insights.speaker: Ilia
insights.so_what: Notable that two infrastructure leaders converge on the same non-obvious, politically difficult solution (tail-emission) rather than the more commonly discussed binary of 'freeze vs. do nothing' -- worth tracking whether this option gains traction in Bitcoin governance discourse.

insights.claim: Charles argues the worst possible outcome is not any single chosen policy but a failure to reach social consensus at all: if urgency spikes only once an actual quantum attack is imminent or underway, Bitcoin could fracture into competing hard-forks, each defended by a different camp, causing more damage than any single agreed-upon policy.
insights.speaker: Charles
insights.so_what: A chain-split/hard-fork scenario triggered by a rushed, crisis-driven quantum response is a distinct tail risk from the three Satoshi-coin options themselves -- position sizing and custody planning should account for possible fork risk around any future quantum-threat event, not just a single 'chosen' outcome.

insights.claim: Both guests separately conclude that Bitcoin's informal, slow-moving governance (no formal on-chain mechanism, reliant on miner/developer/user rough consensus) makes it structurally unlikely to proactively resolve the Satoshi-coins question well in advance; Ilia expects it will ultimately come down to miners reactively choosing between binary options only once forced by an active threat.
insights.speaker: Ilia
insights.so_what: Investors should not expect a proactive, orderly Bitcoin quantum-migration policy decision before a live crisis forces one -- plan for a reactive, possibly contentious governance event rather than a calm multi-year migration roadmap.

insights.claim: Host Laura Shin recounts that when she previously interviewed a Bitcoin Core developer (Matt Carallo) about these same quantum-migration questions, his answers deferred to 'the Bitcoin community will decide' without offering concrete positions, which she found unsatisfying and cited as evidence of Bitcoin's governance uncertainty on this issue.
insights.speaker: Laura Shin (host)
insights.so_what: Independent, on-record corroboration from a separate interview that core Bitcoin developers themselves are not yet committing to a quantum-migration plan -- a governance-readiness gap worth monitoring via Bitcoin Core mailing lists/BIPs rather than assuming it's already being handled.

themes.theme: The Seed-Phrase Escape Hatch and Its Limits

insights.claim: An emerging mitigation lets a user prove via a zero-knowledge proof that they possess their original seed phrase (rather than proving control through the public/private keypair itself) as an alternative access path a quantum computer cannot break -- because a quantum attack via Shor's algorithm only breaks the link between a public key and its private key, not the separate link between a seed phrase and the keys it derives.
insights.speaker: Ilia
insights.so_what: A concrete, non-obvious technical mitigation that could let holders protect at-risk assets without a full chain-wide migration, provided their wallet/chain adopts ZK-seed-phrase-proof support -- worth tracking which wallets implement it.

insights.claim: This zero-knowledge seed-phrase escape hatch does not help pre-seed-phrase-standard (pre-BIP-39) legacy coins, including much of Satoshi-era Bitcoin, because seed phrases as a standard did not exist when those addresses were created -- meaning the oldest, most symbolically significant BTC is structurally excluded from this mitigation and remains fully exposed to whichever freeze/tail-emit/do-nothing policy Bitcoin eventually chooses.
insights.speaker: Charles
insights.so_what: Reinforces that Satoshi-era coins face an unusually hard version of the migration problem with fewer available mitigations than typical modern wallets -- a structural reason to expect this specific supply to be at the center of Bitcoin's eventual quantum policy debate.

insights.claim: NEAR already runs continuous cross-chain anomaly detection to catch and block movement of stolen funds -- including attribution to actors such as North Korea-linked hackers -- and expects this same infrastructure will need to be extended specifically to flag coins fleeing a quantum-compromised chain as they attempt to launder through cross-chain swaps.
insights.speaker: Ilia
insights.so_what: Positions NEAR's cross-chain infrastructure (via NEAR Intents) as a potential chokepoint/monitoring layer for laundering proceeds of a future quantum theft event -- a differentiated security narrative versus chains without native cross-chain monitoring.

insights.claim: Both guests state that once a given blockchain becomes fully post-quantum secure, they will continue supporting a separate, still-vulnerable chain rather than dropping it, as long as that chain's insecurity doesn't compromise the security of assets on the migrated chain -- leaving the decision to keep holding a vulnerable asset entirely up to the individual user.
insights.speaker: Charles
insights.so_what: Neither major hardware wallets nor cross-chain custody platforms are likely to force users off a lagging chain via delisting -- expect vulnerable legacy assets to remain freely transactable and supported well past the point their underlying chain is known to be quantum-exposed.
